vignette:
Leila is thirty-six years old. She works on a construction site in the suburbs, operating a forklift and hauling bundles of rebar across the muddy lots. She has been married to Rami for eleven years. They have two children, a girl and a boy. She used to come home smelling like diesel and sweat, and she would joke that the real foundation of their house was the calluses on her palms.

Two years ago, Leila developed a fever that would not break. She ignored it for three days because the crew was pouring a foundation and she could not miss her shift. By the fourth day she was on the floor of the emergency room, and a doctor told her that her kidneys were failing and that sepsis had set in from an infection she had not even known she had. She remembers the way the fluorescent lights buzzed overhead. She remembers Rami's hand gripping hers so hard that her wedding ring cut into her finger. She remembers thinking that she might never see her daughter's first recital or her son's next birthday.

She spent six weeks in the hospital. Two of those weeks were in the intensive care unit, sedated and on a ventilator. When she woke up, she could not move her legs for three more days. The infection had caused a cascade of organ damage that took months to reverse. She had to learn to walk again, to hold a fork, to breathe without feeling like someone was sitting on her chest.

Now it is two years later. Leila is back at work, but she does not drive through the neighborhood where the hospital is located. She takes a longer route to the construction site, even if it adds twenty minutes to her commute. She cannot explain why-she just knows that the sight of the hospital's blue awning makes her chest tighten and her vision darken at the edges. She has stopped going to the grocery store near that part of town. She asks Rami to buy her cold medicine, too, because the pharmacy aisle reminds her of the smell of antiseptic and the sound of the IV pump clicking.

On the job site, she is always looking over her shoulder. She checks the safety harness three times before she climbs onto the scaffolding, even though she has never had an accident. She hears the sound of her own breath and it reminds her of the ventilator, and sometimes she has to stop what she is doing and place her hand on her chest just to feel the beat of her heart. Her supervisor told her last week that she flinches when he taps her on the shoulder. He meant it as a joke, but Leila saw the worry in his eyes.

At night she cannot sleep. She lies beside Rami and watches the numbers on the clock change. She replays the moment the doctor said the word sepsis over and over, like a film stuck on a single frame. When she does fall asleep, she dreams that she is drowning in a room full of beeping machines. She wakes up covered in sweat, her heart racing. She gets up and drinks a glass of water and stands in the kitchen until the shaking stops. She does not tell Rami about the dreams anymore, because he gets that tired look on his face and she does not want him to worry.

She has stopped going to the mosque on Fridays. She used to sit in the back row and feel the peace of the prayers wash over her. Now she cannot stand the close press of bodies or the way the air feels still and warm. She tells her mother-in-law that she is busy with work, and her mother-in-law sighs and says the children need their mother's faith. Leila does not argue. She does not argue about anything that requires her to explain the way her body feels-like a cage, like a clock that might stop at any second.

Her daughter asked her last week why she keeps the bathroom door open when she showers. Leila said it was because the steam made her dizzy. But it is not that. It is that when the door is closed and the water runs, she cannot hear the rest of the house, and she thinks she might stop breathing and no one would know until it was too late. So she leaves the door open a crack, and she keeps her phone on the edge of the sink, and she showers in three minutes flat.

Leila is at work today. She is unloading a truck of lumber. Her hands are steady, but her mind is not. She feels the thrum of the engine in her chest and it reminds her of the ventilator again. She tells herself that she is fine, that two years is a long time, that the doctors said she is healthy. But the feeling does not go away. It sits in her stomach like a stone, and she knows it will be waiting for her when she gets home.
